description: Ohio's joint filing credit (ORC 5747.05(E)) requires EACH spouse to have $500+ of qualifying income -- Ohio AGI excluding interest, dividends, capital gains, rents and royalties, so pensions, IRA distributions, unemployment and other income all count. Those sources are carried at tax-unit level with no per-spouse split, so neither model can evaluate the statutory test and each substitutes an assumption: we use an earned-income proxy (ei1/ei2) and deny, TAXSIM treats unit-level pensions, nonprop and UI as satisfying the low-earning spouse and grants. Probe-confirmed against TAXSIM-35 2026-08-22 on synthetic OH joint returns holding total income fixed: with a spouse at $0 the credit is off, at $600 of spouse wages it is on, and adding unit-level pensions, nonprop or UI turns it on with the spouse still at $0 (spouse business income flips only above ~$2-5k, matching neither the statute nor $500). Supersedes the earlier annotate row, which scoped this to the ~150/yr sitting exactly at the $650 cap: the cap cluster is only the capped tail, and diff/tax on the uncapped remainder lands on 5.000/10/15/20 percent -- the JFC rate schedule -- across ~450 more records a year. The divergence is the attribution assumption, not either encoding
expected_magnitude: 5-20% of tax net of preceding credits, capped $650 per joint return
predicate: filing_status == 2 & pmin(ei1, ei2) < 500 & (txbl_pens_dist + txbl_ira_dist + ui + other_inc + alimony) >= 500
source: OH JFC qualifying-income probe 2026-08-22 (output/probe/oh_jfc_source.R, oh_jfc_source2.R, oh_jfc_sweep.R)

description: T36: TAXSIM phases Connecticut's pension/annuity subtraction (14% TY2019, 28% TY2020) and Social Security subtraction out linearly above the federal-AGI threshold -- from $100,000 to $200,000 for joint and head-of-household filers, $75,000 to $150,000 for single -- where Connecticut applies a cliff: the 2019 CT-1040 booklet allows the 14% subtraction only to filers 'with federal AGI of less than $100,000' (joint) / 'less than $75,000', and the Social Security Benefit Adjustment Worksheet switches to the 25%-taxable rule at those amounts. description: TAXSIM reports a positive DE itemized deduction (v35_state_itemized_deduction) for filers whose federal itemized deductions are entirely zero, and uses it because it exceeds Delaware's small standard deduction. The amount is the SALT cap: $10,000, or $5,000 for married filing separately. v34_state_std_deduction_amount is correct throughout ($3,250/$6,500, matching 30 Del. C. 1108(a)), so only the itemized figure is fabricated. The share of DE records with v35 > 0 jumps from ~54% in 2017-2018 to 97.0% in 2019-2020. TAXSIM therefore runs LOW by the marginal rate on the excess: flat point masses of $445.50 (single, 6.6% bracket, $6,750 of base) and $231.00 (joint, $3,500), the two largest masses in the DE comparison. See research/state_tax/cross_model/external_model_issues.md T10. The predicate keys on TAXSIM having used an itemized deduction where we did not itemize, so it is precise to the affected records rather than dropping a whole population (the MD 2019 lesson)
expected_magnitude: $231-$446 per affected return; 3-16% of DE records by year
source: DE TAXSIM triage 2026-08-13 (TAXSIM v34/v35/v36 read directly on zero-component records)

description: Companion to the T10 row, opposite-signed. Delaware's PIT-RSA carries that class on its own Line 16 and the DE base is the federal Schedule A total less state income taxes, so it belongs and we include it -- TAXSIM runs HIGH here, the reverse of T10. ANNOTATED, NOT EXCLUDED, for two reasons: the affected population is 21-30% of DE records and the identity is only demonstrable on 45% of them; and the same test on CA/DC/MD/MN/NM/VA gives 2-20% identity shares with residuals of both signs, so whether TAXSIM omits the class for those states is OPEN -- MD and MN have already been through attribution and their scores should not move as a side effect of a DE investigation. source: DE MFJ deduction-gap triage 2026-08-13 (v35 vs st_item_ded less other_item_ded, exact on 44.9%)

description: TAXSIM grants Delaware's pension exclusion where Delaware disqualifies it. State-AGI gaps are exact multiples of the statutory $2,000 (under 60) and $12,500 (60+) amounts, so both sides apply the same provision and disagree on eligibility. TAXSIM (a) grants the $2,000 against EARLY IRA distributions -- PIT-RES Line 6 says an early distribution "does not qualify" and every distribution under age 59.5 is early -- and (b) grants it to filers with no retirement income at all, driving state AGI NEGATIVE: 619-642 DE records per year have v32_state_agi < 0 where ours is >= 0, including age-80 records with zero total income where TAXSIM reports -1,999.99. Annotated because the cause columns (txbl_ira_dist, and age relative to 59.5) are not in the harness record frame. See T12. Switched to exclude 2026-10-15 under the close rule: the Delaware DOR FAQ confirms early distributions do not qualify and the exclusion needs pension or eligible retirement income; keyed on exact $2,000 multiples of the state-AGI gap
expected_magnitude: $2,000-$4,000 of base per affected return; ~26% of DE records carry an AGI gap
predicate: abs(st_agi - v32_state_agi) > 50 & abs((st_agi - v32_state_agi) / 2000 - round((st_agi - v32_state_agi) / 2000)) < 0.001
source: DE state-AGI triage 2026-08-13 (exact 2,000/12,500 multiples; v32 < 0 count; record-level profiles)

The -$12,500 / -$21,000 gap groups are TAXSIM's age handling (T57). source: DE state-AGI triage 2026-08-13 (income composition of the -12,500 group)

description: TAXSIM applies Oklahoma's $17,000 itemized cap (68 O.S. 2358(D)(1), TY2018+) as a FLAT cap, without the statutory exemptions for charitable contributions and medical expenses. v35_state_itemized_deduction equals exactly 17,000 on 91% of OK itemizer records in every cap year, and "our itemized = TAXSIM 17,000 + charity + medical" holds exactly to the dollar on 69% of them (median residual 0). TY2017 is the control: no cap existed, TAXSIM never sits at 17,000, and the identity has no hits. TAXSIM therefore runs HIGH. The predicate keys on the failure itself -- TAXSIM pinned at the flat cap while ours exceeds it, which is only possible when the exemptions were dropped. Excluding lifts OK from 0.727/0.719/0.720 to 0.872/0.869/0.873 in TY2018/2019/2020. See T13

source: OK itemized triage 2026-08-13 (v35 pinned at 17,000; identity exact on 69%)

description: OUR-SIDE, pre-registered. DC's Low Income Credit (47-1806.04(e), repealed after TY2017): nonrefundable, table-driven, mutually exclusive with the DC EITC. In TY2019, after repeal, only 479 such records remain. NOTE FOR TRIAGE: this is NOT what makes DC 2017 weak. Because the credit is nonrefundable it is absorbed at low liability, so the affected records match at about 78% -- ABOVE the DC 2017 average of 47% -- and removing them makes the year WORSE (0.471 -> 0.411). source: DC 2017 credit-stage triage 2026-08-13 (credit gap vs v40 on non-EITC records)

description: TAXSIM applies the Form 1 line 11 payroll/retirement-contribution deduction as a $2,000 cap PER RETURN rather than per person. description: TAXSIM grants a flat $2,000 Form 1 line 11 payroll deduction to ANY Massachusetts return with positive gross Social Security, additively on top of any legitimate wage-based deduction, on records that paid no FICA at all. description: The Utah variant of the crosswalk-exposure class (DC/CA). Utah has no state itemized deduction, so the st_itemizing-keyed predicate the other nine states use never fires here -- but UC 59-10-1018(1) builds the taxpayer tax credit base from the FEDERAL deduction less the state income tax deducted on Schedule A, so exactly the same unstripped SALT lands in a credit base instead of a deduction. The crosswalk hands TAXSIM as-reported salt_inc_sales + salt_pers inside otheritem, where no state calculation can identify them as state income tax to add back; TAXSIM adds and then strips its own iterated state tax instead, leaving our as-reported SALT inside its Utah credit base and inflating its credit. Diagnosed 2026-08-22: state AGI and state taxable income agree with TAXSIM to the dollar, the entire difference is st_ded_credit vs v40, and it is confined to federal itemizers (miss rate 0.04% for non-itemizers against 39.2% for itemizers in 2017). Inverting both credits on real records, the implied base gap tracks salt_inc_sales at a median ratio of 0.962. A controlled probe confirms TAXSIM does apply the addback for SALT it can see: given only mortgage and proptax, its implied base is 15,999.94 against the 16,000 supplied. Our encoding is correct; the crosswalk cannot give TAXSIM what the addback needs. Predicate adds a materiality bound the state-itemizing rows do not need: the credit is 6% of the base, so exposure below about $1,667 cannot move liability by the $100 tolerance, and without it a federal-itemizing predicate would exclude a larger share than any state in the class
expected_magnitude: 6% of the unstripped SALT carried into the credit base, before the 1.3% phase-out

description: PolicyEngine deducts HAWAII'S OWN INCOME TAX on the Hawaii return and never applies the Worksheet A-2 disallowance. Sweep (2018, head of household, 2 children, earned = AGI): TAXSIM's v39 matches ours to $22,000 and falls short from there, by exactly 10.82% x (26,360 - 22,230) = $446.87 through the phase-out; the same in 2017 ($438.21), 2019 ($444.15) and 2020 (1,261.75 = the one-child-threshold value at $32,000). Joint filers are right in every year. Keyed where the gap exceeds $100: non-joint, 2+ dependents, greater of earned income or AGI above the one-child threshold + $925 and below the two-child threshold + $19,000 (where both models reach zero). 2019-2020 heads of household are already excluded by T20
expected_magnitude: 10.82% (2017-18) / 10.5% (2019-20) of the threshold gap: $438-$448 at full effect
source: MN triage 2026-09-30 (TAXSIM sweep + statute; hits match 0.129 / 0.087; cells after T20/T21: 2017 0.906 -> 0.925, 2018 0.913 -> 0.932)

description: T23: TAXSIM pays the Minnesota Working Family Credit to CHILDLESS filers aged 65 and over in 2019-2020. Minn. Stat. 290.0671 subd. 1(a)(1) (2019+ text) allows a childless filer who 'has attained the age of 21, but not attained age 65 before the close of the taxable year'; the federal EITC (also zero on every such record) stops at 64 too. TAXSIM 2017-2018 is right (it used federal eligibility then). Keyed where TAXSIM's childless credit can exceed $100: childless, filer 65+ (both spouses on a joint return), earned income over $2,600 and the greater of earned income or AGI under $30,000
expected_magnitude: up to the childless maximum ($279 in 2019, $284 in 2020)

description: T32: TAXSIM pays the Minnesota Working Family Credit to filers whose investment income exceeds the federal EITC limit in 2019-2020 ($3,600 / $3,650). Minn. Stat. 290.0671 subd. 1(a) requires eligibility under IRC 32, which includes the 32(i) disqualified-income test; the 2019 Schedule M1WFC line 1 instructions run the filer through federal EIC Steps 1-5 and waive only the AGI and earned-income limits (Steps 1, 4, 5), not Step 2 (investment income); the 2020 instructions print the $3,650 limit. Probe (2026-10-07; single, 40, $6,000 wages, $5,000 dividends): TAXSIM's own federal EITC is zero but v39 = 188.60 (2019) / 191.40 (2020); in 2018 v39 = 0 (TAXSIM tied the credit to federal eligibility then, as with T23). Keyed where the credit can exceed $100: investment income over the year's limit, earned income over $2,600, and the greater of earned income or AGI under $57,000 (the 2019-2020 three-child joint income limit)
expected_magnitude: up to the WFC maximum for the family size
predicate: eitc_inv_inc > if_else(year == 2019, 3600, 3650) & (ei1 + ei2) > 2600 & pmax(ei1 + ei2, agi) < 57000
source: MN triage 2026-10-07 (the investment-income limit added to our WFC moved 5 / 4 clean 2019 / 2020 records from match to miss; all 9 are this pattern)

M1PR is a separate claim paid by the Department of Revenue outside the income tax; it is not a line of Form M1, and we do not model it (rent and property-tax-refund eligibility are outside our income tax scope, as for the 2024+ renter's credit on the PolicyEngine side). description: T33: TAXSIM's Minnesota marriage credit (Minn. Stat. 290.0675, Schedule M1MA) pools the couple's business income and splits it between the spouses instead of crediting it to the spouse who earned it, although the crosswalk hands each spouse's self-employment income separately (pbusinc/pprofinc vs sbusinc/sprofinc). The credit is keyed to the lesser-earning spouse's own earned income. Probe (2026-10-07), joint, both 45: $100,000 of primary business income and no spouse income gets 230.10 / 206.92 / 210.33 in 2017 / 2019 / 2020, exactly the credit for a $50,000 / $50,000 wage split, while $100,000 of primary wages gets 0; $486,691 of primary business income gets the 2017 maximum 1,430.91. Keyed where a 50/50 split of self-employment income raises the lesser earner's income by more than $1,000 and to at least the M1MA floor ($23,000 in 2017-2018, $25,000 in 2019-2020)
expected_magnitude: up to the marriage-credit maximum ($1,431 in 2017)
predicate: filing_status == 2 & pmin(ei1 - se1, ei2 - se2) + (se1 + se2) / 2 >= if_else(year <= 2018, 23000, 25000) & pmin(ei1 - se1, ei2 - se2) + (se1 + se2) / 2 - pmin(ei1, ei2) > 1000

description: Qualifying older children (M1CWFC, 290.0671 subd. 1: an IRC 32(c) qualifying child aged 18 or over). We count dependents aged 18-23 who are younger than the filer, assuming those aged 19-23 are students. The 18-year-old part is a PolicyEngine bug; the 19-23 part is an unobservable-status assumption.
